speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs (a) how does Singapore assess the increasing alignment of ASEAN and Asia Pacific countries with security and economic blocs dominated by major powers; (b) what strategic considerations guide Singapore's approach to alignment with these blocs; (c) how sustainable is Singapore's stance of "not choosing sides" in the current geopolitical landscape; and (d) whether Singapore anticipates the need for closer ties with specific blocs over others to safeguard our interests, while still avoiding overdependence on any one major power.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Groupings, such as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and Five Power Defence Arrangements – each of these has a different and overlapping configuration of members.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And in fact, these have been around for many years, decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Consequently, countries are hedging through these different configurations, amidst a more divided and uncertain global environment.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will keep an open mind on these new constructs and we will continue to watch developments closely, insofar as the impact on Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We must be guided by the fundamental objectives of Singapore's foreign policy – and it is worth reiterating what these are.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, to protect our independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, to secure access to essential supplies – food, water, energy – and to keep air and sea lines of communication open for this purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, to expand economic opportunities for Singaporeans and Singapore companies in order to maintain our relevance to the world and to make a living.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In a more volatile world that is increasingly inimical to the security and survival of small states, like Singapore, we must try to shape global norms by making common cause with as many friends and partners as possible, in order to support multilateralism, the rule of law and, of course, the United Nations (UN) Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This long-standing, consistent and principled approach to foreign policy has served us well and has afforded us the strategic manoeuvring space.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In line with these principles, we have joined, and in fact, played a facilitative role in groupings, such as APEC, IPEF and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement on Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These diverse groupings have allowed us to expand our economic space and to create more opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore is not presently a member of groupings like the Quad or AUKUS or BRICS, but actually, we share excellent ties with the individual members in all these groupings.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of their members also attend the various ASEAN and international fora where we engage one another and work closely on a wide range of issues.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In particular, we want ASEAN to continue to play a central convening role and for our region to have the centre of gravity which brings all the key players together to find common ground and to harness ASEAN's full economic potential.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The East Asia Summit, for example, allowed ASEAN to play this role for the last two decades and is, in fact, the only platform driven by ASEAN, which brings all the key players in our region together; even when these key players do not necessarily get along.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore has thus been a strong advocate for strengthening collaboration within the East Asia Summit under the framework of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And Singapore will continue to be a credible, reliable and predictable partner to all and we will always act in our long-term national interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government ensure that Singapore does not become isolated in a world of rival alignments strongly opposed to each other?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These laws are also unenforceable because we do not have a global policeman.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the Minister concerned that international law maybe diminishing in reliability as a tool to protect our economic and security interests?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And finally, Sir, the Prime Minister recently said that we have to work harder to strengthen our network of friends and partners, to work with like-minded countries to shape international norms and rules, and to find common ground on issues of shared concerns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) make it clearer in its outreach to Singaporeans, including new citizens, which these like-minded countries are, in order to build a stronger understanding of Singapore's strategic interests, especially when external actors may be sowing doubt among our population?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Mr Giam has asked how sustainable is this posture that we have always adopted of not taking sides but upholding principles.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, I will make the point that our current posture is the correct one, is the essential one, given our national circumstances, our geography, our economic and strategic role.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And let me also say with the benefit of some experience that because all the superpowers and regional and middle powers know that Singapore does not aim to take sides, Singapore is always looking for relevance and being constructive, Singapore always calculates things rationally with a long-term horizon and is always an advocate for international law, they also know that therefore, sometimes we will disagree.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And when we disagree, it is not because I am taking the side of your opponent or your rival, but we disagree because that contravenes a principle that Singapore holds dear.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I would say, from my experience, that adopting this posture, in fact, has led to less pressure on us because people know simply hectoring us, pressurising us is not likely to bear fruit, and in fact, it is more likely to make us dig in and hold the line.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I would also say that in order for us to take this position of not taking sides and upholding principles, we need domestic cohesion and consensus, including in this House.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Because if foreign powers believe that they can erode our resolve by dividing us, they will.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Member is quite right that as far as global norms are concerned, security is concerned, there is no global policeman.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And do not ever believe for a moment in foreign affairs that friendship is a shield, that friendship makes you immune to threats.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that is why in a paradoxical way we have no enemies, but we have lots of friends.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Because people know that our relationship is not one of dependency, is not one of sycophancy, is not one of acting on other people's behalf.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We pay for what we need, we defend our interests and we are united in doing so.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Given that we are getting into a more volatile, complicated and threatening world, this ability to stand on our two feet, united as one people, and with sufficient reserves and the wherewithal, both fiscal and strategic, is all the more crucial.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I would say, we make common cause in concentric circles.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Even at a time when the world is turning negative on trade, in ASEAN, we still believe in lowering barriers, promoting economic integration, facilitating more investments in our infrastructure and preparing us for a digital age when we also need to be sustainable and green.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Beyond that, it is the dialogue partners of ASEAN.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: For instance, if you look at the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, which again, creates a zone of greater economic integration with China, Japan, Korea, Australia, New Zealand and us.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Separately, we are also building our ties and our economic ties with another rising middle power called India.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And you would also notice that the Prime Minister and indeed, all Members of Cabinet have had very extensive travel itinerary.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This week, the Prime Minister will be first, in Peru for APEC, then he will go across to Brazil for the G20.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And in all these fora, we try to find like-minded partners depending on the issue concerned.
And for other small states, they find Singapore to be a dependable, reliable resource.

I do not mean a resource just financially, but a resource of thought, leadership, sharing, capability development, human capacity development, teaching a man to catch fish rather than just giving him a fish.

So, I have given a long, extended answer, but I hope Members understand that the posture and the avenues that we have pursued for decades are still fundamentally sound and in fact, all the more relevant, given the current global environment.
